IX.-THE SECOND CONVENTION.
The Convention of 1841 has already been described
in The Diamond of May, 1879. The Second General
Convention was held at Schenectady, July 26 and 27,
1843. The seven Chapters were all represented.
Thirty-six members of the Fraternity were present.
Eev. William H. Wilcox, Delta, was
president. Each
Chapter delegation provided a Secretary whose duty
it was to prepare a report for his own Chapter.
The most important business was the consideration
of the advisability of establishing a Chapter at Ham
ilton College and the initiation of candidates who were
present as a nucleus for said Chapter. This was not
accomplished without long and earnest discussion
both upon advisability and upon the constitutionality
of the Convention doing it without specific consent
of each Chapter. In order to maintain a conservative
spirit the Convention afterwards voted that in its
opinion "no new Chapter be formed hereafter unless
upon very urgent grounds.
"
An application was received from the Kappa Sigma
Theta Society of Wesleyan University asking "to
have their Society transferred into a branch of the Psi
Upssilon." But the objection to forming new Chap
ters except upon urgent grounds had been passed and
so the application was tabled until it could be seen
-whether the grounds were very urgent in this case.
Later it was referred to the Chapters with approval.
A Committee was appointed to suggest amendments
to the Constitution, of which A. H. Eice, Theta, was
chairman. After much discussion as to the power of
the Convention to alter the Constitution it was decid
ed that it had the power but that it was not expedient
to do it and the matter was referred to the parent
Chapter with power to propose a revised Constitution
which should stand unless objected to by one-third the
members of some Chapters within three weeks of the
receipt of a copy of the said document.
A new catalogue was ordered and its execution re
ferred to the Delta and Lambda Chapters. Voted
that each Chapter provide itself with an appropriate
seal. Ordered that the next Convention be held at
Yale College. It being announced that Bro. Dewitt
C. Eumsey of the Delta had deceased, it was "Eesolved. That the usual badge of mourning be worn
for 30 days after the Convention." George L. Ehle
delivered the oration and Daniel Shepherd the poem
of this anniversary.
The Convention of 1841.
The first convention of the Fraternity ever held was
that of 1841 and it met with the Delta, in the chapel
of the New York University, at 2 p. m. , October 22d.
It was called by means of a note printed in the New
York Tribune, and was signed by Clarkson N. Potter,
W. E. Eobinsou, W. P. Breed, and J. M. Phipps.
These represented the four Chapters existing at that
time. Of those who were present, forty-four in num
ber, many have since risen to distinction. There
were the Hon. Wm. Taylor, Judge H. C. Van Vorst,
Hon. Isaac Dayton, Professor D. B. Hagar, Ex-Gov.
A. H. Eice, G. H. Moore, LL. D., William Allen
Butler, Eev. H. M. Scudder, D. D., Eev. A. H.
Clapp, D. D., and Eev. C. H. Hall, D. D. J. W.
Gott, of the Theta, was elected President. Brothers
Spencer, Hall and Breed were made a committee to
draft an order of exercises, and they submitted the
following :
1. Is it advisable to publish a catalogue of all the
members of the Fraternity?
2. Shall "branches" be established in all the col
leges whose reputation is such as to add to that of the
Fraternity ?
3. ShaU. it be made the duty of every branch to cor
respond with the others at least twice a term ?
4. Shall an annual convention be held with literary
exercises ?
Under the first order of business, it was voted that
Brothers Eobinson, Moore and Jackson be general
editors of a catalogue of aU the names and residences,
together with suitable symbols. There was consider
able discussion whether the names in the catalogue
should be arranged each Chapter in an alphabetical
list, or whether each Chapter be arranged according
to the year of initiation. The la,tter method prevailed,
Brothers Moore of the Delta, Clapp of the Beta, Jack
son of the Theta and Phipps of the Sigma, were made
editors of their respective Chapter Hsts. Brothers

OUR PETITIONERS.
The coming convention will be called, after hearing
the report of the committees, to decide upon the fit
ness of The Lehigh University and the University of
Pennsylvania to receive chapters of our
fraternity. I
put the Lehigh institution first as, but for the arrival of
its petition at the latter part of the convention and the
reconsidering of an adverse vote, the Pennsylvania
petition would have been ruthlessly slaughtered.
As many of the brethren may know where the Uni
versity of Pennsylvania holds out, but are in blissful ig
norance as to the exact place to locate The Lehigh Uni
versity, and the proper grade of high schools with
which to class it, a few items under both heads may not
come amiss. In regard to the first point, Pennsylva
nia claims it among its myriads who are pleased to
style themselves colleges : situated at Bethlehem it is
accessible from all points of the compass by means of
three trunk lines that there intersect. Everybody
knows that Bethlehem is the head centre of the Mo
ravian faith and that it is one of the oldest places in
the state. The University, as I have found out, is a
gift from the late Hon. Asa Packer of Mauch Chunk
who, after supporting it during his life, endowed it
by his will with two million dollars, with the under
standing that it was to be a free institution. In doing
this Judge Packer has put it in the power of any per
son to educate himself at the lowest possible cost.
On looking over its catalogue it would seem, on
paper,
that the requirements for entrance were as
high, if not
higher than those of the average of the institutions
where chapters of the fraternity are now established
and also, on paper, very good courses of study in the
arts, science, and the various engineering branches
are laid down. On looking at the number of fresh
men that enter it seems as if their examination was
strict as
notwithstanding the fact that tuition is free
there are
only about seventy in the present freshman
class as I have been told. On looking at the fresh
man classes in years back they average about sixty
and graduate about twenty per cent so that it would

as laid down. I am told however in justice to the
students that a great many of the technical students
leave at the end of junior year to begin a professional

existing.
Their catalogue says that they have 115 acres of

have an athletic ground. The boys seem to have
made good use of this as I am informed that they cap

I find that there are
only two fraternities there and
Chi Pbi has here its only respectable chapter. These

Dear Sir : By a recent number of The Diamond
it seems that the action of the last convention on the
petition for a Chapter at the University of Minnesota
meets with your editorial displeasure. The complaint
is that, the application "was summarily disposed of as
apparently unworthy even of notice ;" that it received
"cavalier treatment," and that there was a discourte
ous and unfair discrimination between it and similar
petitions from the Universities of Pennsylvania and
Lehigh. As a member of the Committee on New
Business, to whose charge was committed the petitions
during the convention, I may perhaps, by your per
mission, be able to dispel a possible misapprehension
as to the quality of the treatment bestowed upon the
Minnesota affair.
Copies of the Minnesota petition and its accompany
ing documents were distributed to the several Chap
ters some weeks before the meeting of the convention,
and in the interval the matter probably had the atten
tion of most of the active members of the Fraternity.
The delegates accordingly were acquainted with the
subject and, knowing the general sentiment of their
respective Chapters, were prepared to act speedily and
intelligently.
Eeference to the convention records of 1881 will
show that the petition was formally presented imme
diately after the convention organized, that it was re
ferred to the Committee on New Business and report
ed adversely at the afternoon session of the first day.
Those who were in attendance will doubtless recall the
protracted and lively debate that followed. The ques
tion having been made the special order for the morn
ing session of the second day, the debate was renewed
at that time, and the adverse report adopted, a major
ity of the Chapters thereby announcing their opposi
tion to the scheme. In the closing hours of the
convention the measure was again brought forward
by its advocates and again negatived. Surely, since
the records prove that in one shape or another the
Minnesota petition had been before the convention at
every session, Minnesota did receive due attention and
was not "summarily disposed of as apparently rmworthy even of notice."
The difference in the treatment accorded to the pe
titions from Pennsylvania and Lehigh is easily
explained. The Pennsylvania apphcation was accom
panied by a petition, signed by Psi Upsilon graduates
residing in Philadelphia, asking not for a Chapter,
but for the appointment only of a Committee of In
quiry. Our Committee, without regard to the merits
of the main application, reported favorably only on
the request of the graduates, and the appointment of
a Committee of Inquiry was duly authorized. The
Lehigh application was presented so late in the course
of business that a recess was taken to enable the Com
mittee to consider it at aU before final adjournment.
We did not have time to read the papers through.
We could not under the circumstances form any opin
ion in regard to it, we could not favor it consistently,
we had to make some report, and we therefore report
ed adversely in order to put the matter before the
convention. Judge Tourgee thereupon persuaded the
convention that Lehigh University apparently pos
sessed something worth investigating and at his insti
gation the adverse report was disagreed to and a
Committee of Inquiry appointed, as in the case of
Pennsylvania.
The difference in treatment lies, then, solely in this,
that the University of Minnesota was the only one
whose merits were in question and upon whose merits
the Fraternity passed a deliberate judgment. The
merits of the two Pennsylvania coUeges have never
been considered. At present, is it not premature to
say that any distinction or discrimination has been
exercised iu their favor ?
Very truly yours,
